title: Design Twitter
description: Brute force to optimized: gathering and sorting all tweets from self and followees versus a max-heap k-way merge over each user's recent tail.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a simplified Twitter. Implement postTweet(userId, tweetId) (compose a new tweet), getNewsFeed(userId) (return the 10 most recent tweet ids from the user and everyone they follow, most recent first), follow(followerId, followeeId), and unfollow(followerId, followeeId).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A sequence of postTweet, follow, unfollow, and getNewsFeed calls"],["Output","getNewsFeed returns up to 10 tweet ids, most recent first, from self + followees"],["Goal","Efficient getNewsFeed by merging only each followee's most recent tweets, not their entire history"],["Constraints","Up to 3*10^4 calls total"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Merge the k most recent items from MULTIPLE already-time-ordered lists\"","A max-heap based k-way merge, taking only the top 10 overall"],["Each user's own tweets are naturally posted in chronological order","Each followee's tweet list is itself already sorted, so only its tail (most recent entries) ever matters for a top-10 merge"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Each user has their own list of tweets in the order they were posted. getNewsFeed(userId) must produce the 10 most recent tweets across the user's own posts AND every person they follow's posts, combined and sorted by recency, most recent first.

blocks.title: Analogy: Merging Several Personal Diaries by Date, Recent-First
blocks.text: Picture several people's personal diaries, each already written in chronological order, and wanting the 10 most recent entries across ALL of them combined. Since each individual diary is already sorted, only the LATEST few entries from each diary could possibly make the final top-10, no need to read every diary cover to cover.

blocks.caption: Each followee's tweets are individually time-ordered; getNewsFeed merges the recent tails of these lists

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: postTweet(1,5), getNewsFeed(1), follow(1,2), postTweet(2,6), getNewsFeed(1), unfollow(1,2), getNewsFeed(1)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Result"],"rows":[["getNewsFeed(1) after postTweet(1,5)","[5]"],["getNewsFeed(1) after following user 2 and their postTweet(2,6)","[6,5]"],["getNewsFeed(1) after unfollowing user 2","[5]"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before merging EVERY tweet ever posted by the user and their followees, notice that since each person's own tweet list is already in chronological order, only the LAST (at most) 10 tweets from each individual list could ever appear in the final top-10 result, letting a k-way merge (via a max-heap) work over a much smaller candidate set.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Each user's tweets are naturally stored in the order they were posted, so the most recent tweets from any single user are always at the END of their list.

Observation 2: For getNewsFeed, at most 10 tweets total are needed, so from EACH relevant user (self plus followees), only their most recent 10 tweets could possibly contribute to the final answer, no more.

Observation 3: Tagging each tweet with a global, monotonically increasing timestamp (simply a counter incremented on every postTweet call) lets tweets from different users be compared directly by recency.

Observation 4: A max-heap (ordered by timestamp) seeded with the most recent tweet from each relevant user's list lets the top-10 merge proceed efficiently: repeatedly pop the globally most recent tweet, and if that user has an earlier tweet still in range, push it next, standard k-way merge technique.

This leads to tagging every tweet with a global increasing timestamp, and for getNewsFeed, merging just each relevant user's most recent (at most) 10 tweets using a max-heap-based k-way merge, taking the top 10 overall.
6. Brute Force Solution
Collect every tweet ever posted by the user and everyone they follow into one list, sort that entire list by timestamp, and take the top 10.
Step by step algorithm

items: For getNewsFeed(userId), gather ALL tweets from the user and every followee, regardless of how far back they go.
Sort this entire combined list by timestamp, descending.
Return the first 10 tweet ids from this sorted list.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Gathering and sorting every tweet directly implements the definition of "most recent 10 overall."
This scans and sorts an unbounded, ever-growing amount of data on every single getNewsFeed call, even though only the most recent few tweets per user could ever matter.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(T log T) per getNewsFeed call, T being the total tweets across all relevant users (potentially very large).
Space: O(T) for the combined list.

Limitation: since only the top 10 overall are ever needed, and each user's own tweets are already individually sorted, a k-way merge using only each user's most recent 10 tweets is far more efficient than sorting everything.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why gathering everything is wasteful: any tweet beyond the most recent 10 from a SINGLE user could never possibly be needed, since at most 10 tweets total are returned, and that user alone already has 10 more recent candidates ahead of it.

The k-way merge approach: seed a max-heap with the most recent tweet from each relevant user (self plus followees); repeatedly pop the globally most recent tweet from the heap, and if the user it came from has an earlier tweet still worth considering (within their own most-recent-10 window), push that next tweet into the heap.

Bounding the candidates: since at most 10 tweets are ever returned, each user only ever needs to contribute UP TO their most recent 10 tweets as candidates, capping the total candidate pool at (number of followees + 1) times 10.

The core idea: a max-heap-based k-way merge over each user's recent-tail tweets, rather than sorting the full combined history.

Tag tweets with a global counter as timestamp. For getNewsFeed, seed a max-heap with the last tweet of each relevant user's list (capped to their most recent 10), pop the top repeatedly (pushing that user's next-earlier tweet if still within range) until 10 tweets are collected or the heap empties.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run: user 1 posts tweet 5, follows user 2, user 2 posts tweet 6

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["getNewsFeed(1) with only tweet 5","[5]"],["After following user 2 and their tweet 6 (newer)","[6, 5]"],["After unfollowing user 2","[5]"]]}

blocks.caption: A max-heap merges just the recent tails of each relevant user's tweet list

blocks.text: Why This Works

Because at most 10 tweets are ever returned, and each user's own tweets are already time-ordered, no tweet BEYOND a user's most recent 10 could ever make the final answer, since that user alone would already contribute 10 more recent candidates first. The max-heap correctly performs a k-way merge: at every step, it extracts the globally most recent tweet remaining among all active candidates, and replaces it with that same user's next most recent tweet (if still relevant), guaranteeing the true top-10 across all users is produced without ever needing to sort a user's full tweet history.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((F + 10) log F) per getNewsFeed, F being the number of followees, since the heap holds at most F+1 entries at a time and at most 10 pops/pushes are needed.
Space: O(F) for the heap, O(total tweets) for the underlying storage.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Gather and sort ALL tweets from self + followees","O(T log T), T potentially huge","O(T)","Correct, but rescans an ever-growing amount of data on every call."],["Max-heap k-way merge over recent tails","O((F + 10) log F) per call","O(F)","The expected, efficient solution."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Design Twitter is a strong example of the "k-way merge of already-sorted lists" technique, recognizing that bounding the output size (top 10) means only a small, bounded number of candidates per source list ever needs consideration.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to include the user themselves (not just their followees) when building the news feed.
Not bounding candidates to each user's most recent 10, instead pulling their entire history into the heap unnecessarily.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A user follows nobody and has posted fewer than 10 tweets","getNewsFeed returns just their own tweets, most recent first."],["unfollow() called on someone never followed","No effect, and later getNewsFeed calls are unaffected by this no-op."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "since output is capped at 10, each source list only ever needs to contribute its 10 most recent items to a k-way merge" demonstrates the key bounding insight clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "merge the top k items from several already-sorted sources", think: a max-heap-based k-way merge, seeded with each source's most recent (or largest) candidate.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you support deleting a specific tweet?
How would you scale getNewsFeed for a user following millions of people?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Merge k Sorted Lists, the general-purpose version of this exact k-way merge technique.
Any "combine the top results from many pre-sorted sources" design problem, such as a distributed search result merger.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Gathering and sorting all tweets costs O(T log T) per call, T being unbounded; the max-heap k-way merge over recent tails costs O((F + 10) log F) per call, F being the number of followees, the standard efficient approach.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: k-way merge via a max-heap, over each relevant user's recent tail of already-sorted tweets.
Core Idea: seed the heap with each user's most recent tweet; repeatedly pop the globally most recent, replacing it with that user's next-most-recent tweet, until 10 are collected.
Time: O(T log T) for the gather-and-sort-everything approach, O((F + 10) log F) for the optimized k-way merge.
Most Important Observation: bounding the output to 10 means each source list only ever needs to contribute its 10 most recent candidates.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known system-design-flavored problem combining hash maps with the k-way merge technique.
One line memory trick: max-heap merge of each followee's most recent tweets, capped at 10.
